Bigotry is the stubborn, closed-minded intolerance of people who are different from you — especially people who belong to a different group based on things like race, religion, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, or political belief. It means holding strong, negative views about such a group, and refusing — often aggressively — to question, reconsider, or soften those views, no matter what.

The key word is intolerance. A bigot doesn't simply disagree with someone or dislike a group — a bigot believes, at their very core, that a certain group of people is inferior, wrong, or unworthy, and they refuse to hear anything that challenges that belief.
Breaking It Down Into Its Essential Parts

To truly understand bigotry, you need to understand its three building blocks working together:

1. A fixed, negative belief about a group. Bigotry is always directed at a category of people — not just one specific person you've had a bad experience with. A bigot decides that all members of a group share the same flaw, simply because of what group they belong to. "All people of that religion are dangerous." "All people of that race are lazy." These sweeping, blanket judgments are the raw material of bigotry.

2. No reasonable basis for the belief. The beliefs that drive bigotry are not formed through careful thought, real evidence, or fair experience. They are formed through fear, ignorance, upbringing, cultural influence, or a desire to feel superior. This is what separates bigotry from a reasoned disagreement. A person might genuinely and thoughtfully disagree with another person's ideas — that is not bigotry. But when the negative belief is irrational, unfair, and based on what someone is rather than what someone does or thinks, it crosses into bigotry.

3. Stubborn refusal to reconsider. This is the most defining quality of bigotry. A bigoted person is not merely ignorant — ignorance can be cured with information. A bigot resists correction. Even when shown clear evidence that their belief is wrong, even when they meet kind, decent people from the group they despise, they hold on. They dismiss, deny, or rationalize. Their mind is, in a very real sense, closed.

Put all three together: bigotry is the rigid, unreasonable, and closed-minded hostility toward a group of people based on who they are, not on any fair evaluation of them as individuals.

At its emotional core, bigotry is a mixture of contempt (looking down on others), fear (often of difference or of the unfamiliar), and pride (a belief that one's own group is inherently better or more correct). The bigot usually feels entirely justified. In fact, most bigots don't recognize themselves as bigots — they believe they are simply telling the truth, or protecting something they value, or being realistic.

This is important to understand: bigotry rarely feels like hatred from the inside. It often feels like certainty.
What Bigotry Can Be Directed At

Bigotry can target virtually any group that can be defined as "different." Common targets include:

  • Race or ethnicity — believing one race is superior or another is inferior
  • Religion — intolerance of people of a different faith (or no faith at all)
  • Gender — contempt for a particular gender
  • Sexual orientation — hostility toward gay, lesbian, bisexual, or other people
  • Nationality — looking down on people from a particular country
  • Social class — treating people as lesser because of how much money they have or don't have
  • Political belief — extreme intolerance of those with opposing political views

Bigotry has no single home. It can exist across every culture, country, class, and ideology. People of any background can hold bigoted views about people of any other background.
Bigotry vs. Related Words You Should Know

These words are neighbors of bigotry and are often confused with it:

Prejudice is the attitude — the unfair, pre-formed negative opinion about a group. Bigotry includes prejudice but goes further: bigotry is prejudice that is stubborn, intense, and actively resistant to change. You could say prejudice is the seed, and bigotry is the deeply rooted tree.

Discrimination is the action — when someone treats a person unfairly because of their group membership (refusing to hire them, serve them, rent to them, etc.). Bigotry is the mindset; discrimination is what can happen as a result of that mindset. One lives in the head; the other plays out in the world.

Racism, sexism, homophobia, etc. are all specific forms of bigotry. Racism is bigotry based on race. Sexism is bigotry based on gender. These words name the particular group being targeted. "Bigotry" is the umbrella term that covers all of them.

Hatred is an intense emotion. Bigotry doesn't always involve conscious hatred — it can show up as dismissiveness, condescension, or quiet contempt. All hatred-fueled behavior against a group involves bigotry, but not all bigotry rises to the level of outright hatred.

Imagine someone who firmly believes that people of a certain religion are all dishonest — not because of any real evidence, but because they grew up hearing it. When they meet a kind, honest person from that religion, they say, "Oh, they're one of the good ones" — and their view of the group doesn't change at all. That resistance to updating their belief, even in the face of direct evidence, is bigotry in action.

Or imagine a person who believes that people from a certain country are all unintelligent. You show them scientists, artists, and leaders from that country. They dismiss them as exceptions. The belief survives every challenge. Again — that is bigotry.

The through-line in every example is the same: a fixed negative view of a group of people, held stubbornly, regardless of reality.

Bigotry is an uncountable noun, which means you typically don't say "a bigotry" or "bigotries." You say:

  • "His bigotry was on full display."
  • "Bigotry has no place in a just society."
  • "She had encountered bigotry her entire life because of her faith."

The related words are bigot (noun — a person who practices bigotry) and bigoted (adjective — describing someone or something characterized by bigotry):

  • "He is a bigot."
  • "That was a bigoted remark."

What makes bigotry particularly damaging — to individuals, to communities, and to societies — is not just that it involves unfair beliefs. It's that it dehumanizes. When you reduce a person to nothing more than their group membership and attach a negative judgment to that membership, you stop seeing them as a full, complex human being. You replace the actual person with a stereotype, and you treat the stereotype rather than the person.

This is why bigotry, across history and across the world, has been at the root of so much injustice — from discrimination and exclusion to violence and persecution. The beliefs may live in the mind, but their consequences land in the real world.
